newsitem.title: CHINA: China reflation seen under way, gaining pace.
newsitem.headline: China reflation seen under way, gaining pace.

text.p: China has begun a long-awaited reflation of its economy, easing credit on a broad front, with credit expansion expected to grow faster in 1997, the research department of merchant bank Kleinwort Benson said.
It said in a report that its analysts were convinced that China's three-year austerity programme was over and that Beijing was more concerned with unemployment than inflation.
"Officials will no longer be able to talk about austerity; that phase is over," said the report. "An 'appropriately tight money policy' has replaced austerity though in reality, credit is easing."

The report, seen by Reuters in Beijing on Monday, was prepared by the company's Singapore-based strategist Hugh Peyman and economist Geoff Lewis after a recent visit to China during which they met with officials in the financial sector.

The report concluded that the policy change was made in August as macro-economic indicators, particularly inflation, came in well within the government's target. Evidence of the change would be more apparent over the next three to six months, it added.

Dai Xianglong, chief of the People's Bank of China, the central bank governor, has forecast inflation at less than 6.6 percent this year -- well within the target of 10 percent and down sharply from 14.8 percent in 1995.

As of the end of September, unemployment was officially at 2.98 percent but that does not include the so-called disguised unemployment of those workers "temporarily laid off" and those still on the payroll with little or nothing to do.
Some economists have estimated that the urban jobless rate could reach 8.0 percent if surplus workers at factories are included.
Lingering problems of money-losing state-run enterprises are contributing to concerns among officials and economists about unemployment problems and the potential for social unrest.
Kleinwort Benson forecast credit expansion of 20 percent to 25 percent next year compared with an expected 17 percent this year.

It said that in the second half of the year an extra 70 billion yuan ($8.43 billion) a month would be injected into the financial system compared with 45 billion yuan a month in the first half. That would rise to 80 billion to 95 billion yuan a month next year.
Political considerations were likely to make the higher end of the range more likely next year, the bank added.
Kleinwort Benson said the central bank had more control over monetary policy than in the past but the ultimate policy decision would be made by the State Council, or cabinet.

Compromises on credit could be expected ahead of a key Communist Party meeting late next year, though it added that credit expansion would likely be reined in afterwards and not be on the scale of that of 1992/93.

The policy shift was confirmed by enterprises in the more liberalised regions of the economy -- the southern province of Guangdong and the port city of Shanghai. Evidence of the shift was scarce elsewhere because banks were lending to enterprises most capable of repaying -- most of them in the economically advanced areas.

The report added that additional liquidity would benefit Hong Kong listed companies though it said greater stock market beneficiaries would be found among manufacturers and traders in South Korea, Taiwan and Japan.
Natural resources firms in Malaysia, Indonesia, the Philippines and Australia would also benefit.
